item.title: 796 coronary angiograms performed at Lautoka Hospital Cath Lab

item.content:encoded:
The Cath Lab at Lautoka Hospital has performed 796 coronary angiograms since commencing the service in May 2025, providing hundreds of Fijians with access to advanced cardiac diagnostic care closer to home.

In a statement, Aspen Medical said a coronary angiogram is the gold-standard imaging procedure used to diagnose coronary artery disease by giving cardiologists a detailed view of the heart’s blood vessels.

The procedure enables doctors to detect blockages, assess heart health and determine the most appropriate treatment at an early stage.

Aspen Medical said the service has allowed many patients to receive accurate and timely diagnoses without the need to travel overseas.

The healthcare provider said every early diagnosis creates an opportunity for earlier treatment, improved health outcomes and greater peace of mind for patients and their families.

Aspen Medical said expanding access to world-class cardiac diagnostic services at Lautoka Hospital is helping transform heart care across Fiji, one patient at a time.

item.title: AI rapidly shifts to operational hazard
item.description: ARTIFICIAL intelligence is rapidly shifting from a technical novelty into an immediate operational hazard, rapidly upskilling threat actors and forcing organisations to overhaul their approach to risk management. National Risk Solution director Chris Graham made these comments while speaking at the Pacific Fiber Conference 2026 in Nadi, saying brokers and underwriters across global hubs from Londo
item.content:encoded:
ARTIFICIAL intelligence is rapidly shifting from a technical novelty into an immediate operational hazard, rapidly upskilling threat actors and forcing organisations to overhaul their approach to risk management.

National Risk Solution director Chris Graham made these comments while speaking at the Pacific Fiber Conference 2026 in Nadi, saying brokers and underwriters across global hubs from London to Singapore had reported that cyber exposures now reached into hundreds of millions of dollars.

The core issue, experts warn, is that tools once locked behind months of specialist dark web collaboration are now broadly accessible.

Mr Graham said AI was effectively arming unsophisticated criminals overnight, accelerating deceptive tactics like targeted phishing and automated fraud.

At the same time, he said companies were eagerly embedding AI into internal workflows to capture efficiency gains.

Yet, he added that rapid adoption had created dangerous blind spots around unapproved employee software, data transfers, and rogue automated agents.

“Risk management cannot remain a once-a-year exercise, cyber risk is now a business loss issue, not only a technical incident,” Mr Graham said.

“It can become downtime, lost money, legal cost, reputational damage, and recovery expense,” he said.

While human error and everyday scams remained frequent drivers of claims, Mr Graham said high-severity events like ransomware continued to dominate organisational losses.

Modern insurance covers must now serve as active resilience tools funding threat monitoring, forensics, and crisis response rather than acting as passive payout policies.

To withstand evolving threats, Mr Graham proposed that leaders must regularly test internal controls, establish clear accountability for AI failures, and present verifiable risk management practices directly to underwriters before severe market losses occur.

item.title: Human-centred AI takes centre stage at fiber conference
item.description: ARTIFICIAL intelligence must serve humanity rather than dominate it, said Minister for Policing and Communications Iowane Naivalurua. While addressing delegates at the Pacific Fibre Conference yesterday at the Sheraton Fiji Resort and Spa in Nadi, Mr Naivalurua reflected on lessons from a recent AI summit in New Delhi, emphasising two fundamental principles for emerging technology.
item.content:encoded:
ARTIFICIAL intelligence must serve humanity rather than dominate it, said Minister for Policing and Communications Iowane Naivalurua.

While addressing delegates at the Pacific Fibre Conference yesterday at the Sheraton Fiji Resort and Spa in Nadi, Mr Naivalurua reflected on lessons from a recent AI summit in New Delhi, emphasising two fundamental principles for emerging technology.

“AI must serve you and I, not the other way around,” he said.

“Second, for AI, we must try and make it as human as possible.”

Mr Naivalurua said that operationalising those values was the primary responsibility facing industry experts gathered in Nadi.

He also confirmed that Fiji had formally endorsed new regional digital and artificial intelligence principles at the Pacific ICT Ministers’ Meeting in Papua New Guinea, awaiting final approval by Pacific leaders.

“These principles will anchor the future of digitalisation and AI in safety, cultural values, and ethical governance tailored to the Pacific Island needs.”

Domestically, Mr Naivalurua said the Government was pairing those policy frameworks with direct technology investments, including a nationwide CCTV initiative initially established in the Central Division.

He said that advanced technical tools were essential to bolster the fight against drugs and other serious crimes.

item.title: Mali chief explains ending tourism agreement
item.description: A TOURISM agreement between the people of Mali Island and international organisation Tribe Wanted was ended after the group failed to honour its agreement with the landowners. Tui Mali Ratu Apenisa Bogiso said Tribe Wanted approached the village back in 2006 seeking to lease Vorovoro Island for three years.
item.content:encoded:
A TOURISM agreement between the people of Mali Island and international organisation Tribe Wanted was ended after the group failed to honour its agreement with the landowners.

Tui Mali Ratu Apenisa Bogiso said Tribe Wanted approached the village back in 2006 seeking to lease Vorovoro Island for three years.

He said before agreeing to the proposal, he had wanted to know how the community would benefit.

“I asked them what benefits will the community receive if you are only staying for three years,” Ratu Apenisa said.

He said the village agreed to the three-year arrangement but when the lease ended, Tribe Wanted asked for another year.

“Instead of discussing the extension with me and the landowners, the organisation held meetings with other people and collected money without my knowledge.

“They were making decisions behind my back, so I decided to end the arrangement.”

Under the project, members of the online community from around the world paid a fee to stay on Vorovoro Island for several weeks and experience village life.

Macuata Tourism Association president Amelia Simmons said the experience showed why future tourism developments must be built on trust, proper consultation and written agreements.

Ms Simmons said any tourism project must have the full support of landowners and how the community would benefit be clearly explained.

Today, the community now hosts university students from the United States through the Bridge the Gap study abroad program, which village leaders say operates with clear agreements and greater involvement from the local community.

item.title: Baravilala: Secure and interoperable cyberspace crucial
item.description: THE fundamental shift in how digital technologies are embraced daily is the very reason that an open, secure, accessible, interoperable, and peaceful cyberspace is crucial. These were the comments of Tupou’tuah Baravilala, director–general for Digital Government Transformation, Cybersecurity and Communications, while addressing attendees of the Pacific Fiber Conference at the Sheraton Fiji Golf Re
item.content:encoded:
THE fundamental shift in how digital technologies are embraced daily is the very reason that an open, secure, accessible, interoperable, and peaceful cyberspace is crucial.

These were the comments of Tupou’tuah Baravilala, director–general for Digital Government Transformation, Cybersecurity and Communications, while addressing attendees of the Pacific Fiber Conference at the Sheraton Fiji Golf Resort and Spa in Nadi last week.

“This has been a key priority for the Fijian Government in ensuring that we are in the right forums globally to shape these technologies,” Ms Baravilala said.

Ms Baravilala’s presentation touched on how digital technologies, when implemented correctly, had revolutionised the world in a very fundamental way.

“The ministry has a unique vantage point where we’re able to see or have visibility how the digital ecosystem works, from guaranteeing and enabling and conducive environment for the private sector, to access to meaningful connectivity, to digital transformation efforts, while at the same time ensuring that we have cybersecurity and data protection provisions in place, and that we have measures in place to combat cybercrime as we all know, which is transboundary in nature.”

Ms Baravilala said those were different but very important pieces of the cyber ecosystem puzzle.

“So take one puzzle piece that we’ve all spoken about, which is making sure that we have an enabling and business conducive ICT infrastructure landscape.

“Twenty-one years ago, only 1 billion people enjoyed access to the internet.

“Today, six billion people are now connected to the internet.

“It means that we’re doing good work in bridging the connectivity divide but it’s not great because we have 2.2 billion people who are still not connected and that’s the priority to ensure that all of our people have universal, but also meaningful connectivity.”

She said ensuring that members of the public had meaningful connectivity remained a key priority for the Government.

item.title: Envoy: Quality over quantity
item.description: THE focus of infrastructure investment in the Pacific should not only be on the amount of funding provided, but on ensuring projects are sustainable, high quality and guided by clear principles. Australian High Commissioner to Fiji Peter Roberts said infrastructure development in the region should be centred on delivering projects that are fit for purpose, avoid unsustainable financial pressures a
item.content:encoded:
THE focus of infrastructure investment in the Pacific should not only be on the amount of funding provided, but on ensuring projects are sustainable, high quality and guided by clear principles.

Australian High Commissioner to Fiji Peter Roberts said infrastructure development in the region should be centred on delivering projects that are fit for purpose, avoid unsustainable financial pressures and support local industries.

Appearing on the Lens@177, Mr Roberts said there were many partners involved in infrastructure development in Fiji and the wider Pacific, including Australia, the Asian Development Bank, other countries and the private sector.

He said the priority should be ensuring communities received quality infrastructure that provided long-term benefits.

“One of the key principles for infrastructure financing was responsible lending,” he said.

“Australia only supports projects where countries were able to manage their financial commitments.”

He said while debt challenges were not an issue in Fiji, there had been situations elsewhere where countries had struggled to repay loans and faced financial pressures.

“Infrastructure projects also need to meet high standards to ensure they remain effective and do not deteriorate due to poor quality construction.”

He added that supporting local industries was another important consideration, highlighting Australia’s work following Tropical Cyclone Winston, particularly the construction of schools on Vanua Levu through local partners.

“I think it’s great to have lots of infrastructure investment in the Pacific, and there’s heaps of players who are keen to do it.

“But I think having those principles is really, important.”

item.title: Australia embraces Pacific identity
item.description: AUSTRALIA now sees itself as part of the Pacific, a shift that has reshaped its approach to engaging with the region. Australian High Commissioner to Fiji Peter Roberts, while on the Lens@177, said Australia’s understanding of its place in the Pacific had evolved significantly over the past two decades, influencing how it works with Pacific island countries, including Fiji.
item.content:encoded:
AUSTRALIA now sees itself as part of the Pacific, a shift that has reshaped its approach to engaging with the region.

Australian High Commissioner to Fiji Peter Roberts, while on the Lens@177, said Australia’s understanding of its place in the Pacific had evolved significantly over the past two decades, influencing how it works with Pacific island countries, including Fiji.

Responding to a question on whether China’s growing presence in the Pacific had made Australia a better partner for the region, Mr Roberts said the biggest change had come from Australia’s own reassessment of its identity and interests.

“So I first joined the Department of Foreign Affairs and trained in Australia 26 years ago and my first posting was Samoa” Mr Roberts said.

“But what I think has really changed in those 26 years I’ve worked is Australia, is a realisation in Australia that we are part of the Pacific and that we’re connected, and that our interests are here.

“Definitely when I joined (Fiji), there was much more focus in other areas.”

Mr Roberts said Australia’s approach was also reflected in the way it viewed regional security, pointing to the adoption of the Ocean of Peace Declaration by Pacific Islands Forum leaders last year.

He said the declaration emphasised addressing security challenges through a Pacific-led response and in the “Pacific way”.

“Australia’s recognition that it was part of the Pacific also meant acknowledging this regional approach and working with Pacific nations collectively on security and other shared issues.”

He said the shift was less about external competition and more about Australia’s recognition that it belonged in the Pacific and shared common interests with its neighbours.

item.title: Fewer workers leaving PALM jobs
item.description: ONLY about 3 per cent of Pacific Australia Labour Mobility (PALM) workers are leaving their jobs early, with the rate continuing to fall. Australian High Commissioner to Fiji Peter Roberts said the declining disengagement rate showed the scheme was improving, while acknowledging there were still cases where workers left their employment and required support.
item.content:encoded:
ONLY about 3 per cent of Pacific Australia Labour Mobility (PALM) workers are leaving their jobs early, with the rate continuing to fall.

Australian High Commissioner to Fiji Peter Roberts said the declining disengagement rate showed the scheme was improving, while acknowledging there were still cases where workers left their employment and required support.

Speaking on The Fiji Times online portal Lens@177, Mr Roberts referred to the recent case of a Fijian PALM worker who disengaged from his job and was found living under a bridge in Australia earlier this year.

“Its down to about 3 per cent of people leave their employment. If possible, we want to support those people to re-engage, find another job,” he said.

“If not, then we have to all work with the community liaison officers and others to support those people because we don’t want anybody in tough situations.”

He said Australia had also strengthened compliance measures to ensure employers met their obligations.

Mr Roberts noted that PALM workers were entitled to the same employment conditions as Australian workers.

“That’s the rule. There’s a strong compliance system now because this isn’t PALM specific.

“In any sector, sometimes there are employers who don’t do the right thing.”

Mr Roberts said while some employers across different industries failed to do the right thing, compliance systems, community liaison officers and a 24-hour helpline were in place to respond to workplace issues and support workers facing difficulties.

“We don’t want anybody in tough situations.”
